title: CRISPR: Editing Genes

endcard.line: Pictures: NIH Image Gallery (public domain); PantheraLeo1359531 (CC0)

segments.say: Biology's most talked-about tool of this century was borrowed from bacteria.

anim.title: How bacteria do it
items: Bacteria keep a piece of its DNA
They make RNA that matches it

segments.say: When a virus attacks, some bacteria save a piece of its DNA. If it returns, they make RNA that matches it, and an enzyme called Cas9 cuts the virus apart.

anim.title: In the lab
items: It leads Cas9 to one spot
The cell repairs: add, delete or replace

segments.say: Scientists copied the trick. They write a guide RNA for the gene they want, Cas9 cuts there, and the cell's own repair system adds, deletes or replaces DNA.
That makes CRISPR simpler, faster and cheaper than older gene-editing methods, and more precise.
It is being tested against inherited diseases such as sickle cell disease, haemophilia and cystic fibrosis. Sickle cell is a big concern in parts of India.
Most work edits ordinary body cells, which affects only that person. Editing eggs, sperm or embryos would pass changes to future generations, and that raises hard ethical questions.
For Prelims and GS Three, remember the pair: the guide RNA finds the spot, and Cas9 cuts it.

sources: MedlinePlus Genetics (US National Library of Medicine), 'What are genome editing and CRISPR-Cas9?': adapted from a bacterial defence; bacteria store virus DNA in CRISPR arrays, make matching RNA, and Cas9 cuts the virus DNA; researchers make a guide RNA plus Cas9 to cut a target, and the cell's repair machinery adds, deletes or replaces DNA; faster, cheaper, more accurate and more efficient than other methods; studied for cystic fibrosis, haemophilia and sickle cell disease; most changes are in somatic cells; germline editing raises ethical concerns
NHGRI, genome editing page: CRISPR is simpler, faster and cheaper than earlier methods

quiz.q: In CRISPR-Cas9, what does Cas9 do?
options: Cuts the DNA at the target
quiz.why: The guide RNA finds the spot; Cas9 cuts; the cell repairs.

quiz.q: Where did the CRISPR idea come from?
quiz.why: It is adapted from how bacteria fight viruses.

quiz.q: Why does germline editing raise ethical concerns?
options: It is slower than somatic editing
Its changes can pass to future generations
quiz.why: Edits to eggs, sperm or embryos are inherited.

reviewNote: Facts were read against MedlinePlus Genetics and NHGRI. 'Sickle cell is a big concern in parts of India' is general knowledge, not from those sources; cut it or add a source (for example the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission on PIB) before approval. Moving facts: approved CRISPR therapies are changing; none is named.
